node-1.label: Patient in their 70s presented with dyspnea and fatigue

node-2.label: Medical history: no structural heart disease or hypertension; diffuse large B-cell lymphoma diagnosed 4 years ago, treated with 8 courses of chemotherapy

node-3.label: Physical examination: blood pressure 96/54 mm Hg, heart rate 56 bpm

why.why: Radiologist and pathologist analyses both explicitly state that echocardiography showing diffuse right atrial masses, PET-CT hypermetabolism along the right atrial myocardium/pericardium, ECG suggesting atrial infiltration, and only mildly elevated troponin are more consistent with myocardial infiltration by lymphoma than with chemotherapy cardiotoxicity. The structural and metabolic imaging evidence therefore directly refutes chemotherapy cardiotoxicity as the primary cause, though prior anthracycline exposure cannot be entirely excluded.

The available imaging and laboratory findings—diffuse right atrial masses, PET-CT hypermetabolism along the right atrial myocardium/pericardium, ECG changes suggesting atrial infiltration, and elevated NT-proBNP—are strongly supported by both the radiologist and pathologist analyses as evidence of lymphoma relapse. Confidence is increased, but histopathological biopsy/immunohistochemistry and pericardial fluid cytology/flow cytometry are still pending, so definitive pathological confirmation remains unavailable.

The pathologist analysis explicitly states that endocrine/metabolic disorder lacks support, and the radiologist analysis explains the hypotension, bradycardia, and fatigue through cardiac lymphoma involvement. The structural right atrial mass and PET-CT hypermetabolism provide a more coherent explanation than an endocrine/metabolic disturbance, so this hypothesis remains unlikely.

The pathologist analysis states that sepsis/opportunistic infection also lacks support, and the radiologist analysis attributes the hemodynamic findings to cardiac involvement. Bradycardia remains atypical for sepsis, and the demonstrated right atrial/pericardial lymphoma involvement better explains the clinical picture. Thus, sepsis/opportunistic infection is very unlikely.
